habit_line: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome back, inquirers! In Secondary 1 you will meet numbers that go below zero. You already know some: the freezer, a winter holiday in Japan, the basement car park. Today we find out how they behave, and we make the computer go below zero too.
Notice it, test it, explain why. Today "test it" means test it in Scratch.
do: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Here are five cities at 7 a.m. on a December morning. Put them in order from coldest to warmest. Beijing is −9 and Seoul is −7. Nine is bigger than seven, so which is colder? Argue with your partner.
How many degrees warmer is Tokyo than Seoul? How did you count it?
Your sprite is at x = 0. It changes x by 100, then changes x by −250. Where will it be? Write your prediction before you test it.
The thermometer starts at 5 and goes down 3, six times. What is the last number it will say? Write it down first.
stuck: Stuck: drag the sprite left and right and watch the x number under the stage. Left of the middle is negative.
Wrong prediction: draw a number line on your whiteboard and do the six jumps of 3. Where do you cross 0?
Finished early: make the sprite walk with the temperature (set x to temp × 10), or add "if temp < 0 then say Below zero!".

say: “It is −4 °C and it rises 9 degrees. Rising means moving right. From −4 it takes 4 to get to 0. I still have 5 of my 9 left, so I land on 5 °C.”
“Change temp by −4 means I add negative 4. Adding a negative moves me left, so it is the same as taking away 4: 1 + (−4) = 1 − 4 = −3.”
“7 − (−3) asks how far it is from −3 to 7. From −3 up to 0 is 3, from 0 up to 7 is 7. That is 10 steps right, so the answer is 10. Check: −3 + 10 = 7.”

do: Ask: “Which way did you move? Where did you cross zero?”
Ask: “How can you check your answer by adding back?”
Ask: “In your trace table, which row is the start and which rows are the repeats?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a number line and mark 0 first.”
Hint 2: “Split the jump at 0: how far to 0, and how far after it?”
Hint 3: “For a − b, start at b and count to a. Right means a positive answer, left means a negative answer.”

say: “Ben says −8 is bigger than −3 because 8 is bigger than 3. Is he right?”
“Why does change by −3 make a number go down?”
ask: “Ben says −8 is bigger than −3 because 8 is bigger than 3. Is he right?”

Ben is not right. −8 is further left on the number line, so it is smaller: −8 °C is colder than −3 °C and floor −8 is lower than floor −3. The digit tells us how far from 0, the sign tells us which side. Change by −3 adds a negative, which moves left, so it is the same as taking away 3.

say: “Today you went below zero on paper and in code. In Secondary 1 these are called negative numbers or integers, and you already know how to move with them. Well done, inquirers!”

p6l3-title.note: Objective: Order and compare negative numbers on a number line; add and subtract with negative numbers by moving along the line (temperature, lifts, sea level); use "change by" a negative number in code and trace a variable that goes below 0. Materials: laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 open (scratch.mit.edu, no log-in needed), mini whiteboard and marker, workbook, pencil. Tutor: this deck, Scratch open for screen share. Online set-up: children keep Scratch in one browser tab and the video call in another; ask them to rename the sprite "Dot" so nobody is distracted by costumes. Children share their screen only when asked. Type the minus sign with the keyboard minus key (the hyphen); do not copy and paste a number from the slide or chat, because the slide uses a different minus character that Scratch will not accept. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 5.5, warm-up 5.5 to 11.5, explore at the computer 11.5 to 26.5, mini-lesson 26.5 to 36.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41.5, worksheet 41.5 to 74.5 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 74.5 to 77.5 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 77.5 to 83.5, exit slip 83.5 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. SPINE: Today's tool is Draw it. Sketch and label a model; let the picture show what stays the same. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p6l3-check.note: Minutes 2 to 5.5. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: −2 °C (3 down to 0 is 3 degrees, then 2 more below zero). A drawn thermometer or number line shows it. Puzzle 2: 22 degrees. From −18 up to 0 is 18, then 4 more: 18 + 4 = 22. A number line drawing shows it. Guessing is fine. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l3-warm1.note: Minutes 5.5 to 9. Cold city line-up. Give each child a city (online: type the city names in the chat in order, coldest first, then reveal). Ask: "Which is colder, Beijing at −9 or Seoul at −7? Nine is bigger than seven, so why is −9 colder?" Let them argue before any click. Click 1 puts the cities on the number line (Har = Harbin, Bei = Beijing, Seo = Seoul, Tok = Tokyo, Sin = Singapore). Click 2 shows the order. Click 3 shows the gap Tokyo to Seoul: from −7 up to 0 is 7, then up to 3 is 3 more, 10 degrees. Keep it to about 150 seconds: the order and the Tokyo to Seoul gap only (the Singapore to Harbin extra is cut). Watch for children who say −9 is warmer than −7 because 9 > 7: we fix this with the number line in a moment.

p6l3-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 11.5. Whiteboards: write, say the answer together on three, then click. Three questions only. Answers: 1) −2 °C (3 down to 0, then 2 more). 2) −7 °C (further below 0). 3) B3. Ask: "Where have you seen numbers below zero?" (freezer, weather apps for Japan or Korea, basement lifts, golf scores, a bank balance that is overdrawn, sea level.)

p6l3-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 26.5 (this slide 11.5 to 16). SAY OUT LOUD at the start of the explore: "Type the minus sign with the minus key on your keyboard. Do not copy and paste it from the slide or the chat, because Scratch will not accept the pasted one and you would think you were wrong." Screen-share Scratch for 1 minute: show the x number under the stage as you drag the sprite left and right. "The stage is a number line. The middle is 0. Left of the middle is negative." Then children work in pairs (breakout rooms online), each on their own computer. Step 2: Dot starts at 0, change x by 100 takes it to 100, change x by −250 takes it to −150. Step 3: make the variable live in your screen share: Variables, Make a Variable, type temp, OK (children copy you). Type negative numbers with the keyboard minus key, never by pasting from the slide. There is no "decrease" block: to go down you change by a negative number. Step 4: they must write the prediction on the whiteboard BEFORE clicking. The program says 2, −1, −4, −7, −10, −13. Anyone who wants more: add "if temp < 0 then say Below zero!" inside the loop, or make Dot glide to x = temp × 10 each time so it walks along the stage. Optional Python version (same program, for children who know Python): temp = 5 | for hour in range(6): | temp = temp + (-3) | print(temp) Output: 2, -1, -4, -7, -10, -13 (one per line). Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if the thermometer program starts at 5 and repeats 20 times (change temp by −3 each time)? Predict the last number. Which repeat number first gives a number below −30? Answer: −55 (5 − 3 × 20). Below −30 first happens at repeat 12: 5 − 36 = −31 (repeat 11 gives −28).

p6l3-explore2.note: Minutes 16 to 26.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather them to answer. Answers: 1) x = −150 (100 − 250: from 100 back to 0 is 100, then 150 more). 2) −13 (5, then 2, −1, −4, −7, −10, −13: six jumps of 3 down). Many predict −12 or −18: ask them to count the jumps on a number line. 3) Change it by a negative number: "change temp by −3" moves it 3 to the left. Adding a negative is the same as taking away.

p6l3-teach1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 28.5. Teach. Click 1: the three points. Ask: "Which is biggest? Which is smallest?" Then the steps. Think-aloud: "Six is bigger than one, but MINUS 6 is further below zero than minus 1. If I owe you $6, I am poorer than if I owe you $1." Use the signs: < means "is less than", pointing at the smaller number. Common slip: ordering by the digits only.

p6l3-we1.note: Minutes 28.5 to 30.5. Click order: the +9 jump, the −7 jump, step 1, step 2. Ask before each jump: "Which way do we move? Where do we cross zero?" Think-aloud: "Rising means moving right. From −4 it takes 4 to reach 0. I still have 5 of my 9 left, so I land on 5. Falling means moving left: 5 to get down to 0, 2 more to −2." Splitting the jump at 0 is the key move.

p6l3-try1.note: Minutes 30.5 to 31.5. Whiteboards. a) 6 up to 0, then 4 more: 4. b) 3 down to 0, then 5 more: −5. c) Already below zero, keep going left 6: −8. Children who write 8 or −4 for c have moved the wrong way: "Take away means move left."

p6l3-teach2.note: Minutes 31.5 to 32.5. Teach. Point at the red "change temp by −4" block from explore. "We are adding, but we are adding a negative, so we move left." Click: the jump, step 1, the summary. Ask: "What will the sprite say?" (−3). Brackets: we write 1 + (−4) so the two signs do not crash into each other.

p6l3-we2.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34.5. Click order: the jumps, step 1, step 2, the answer. Think-aloud: "Subtraction finds the difference. 10 − 4 = 6 because from 4 to 10 is 6. The same works below zero: from −3 to 7 is 10." Right means a positive answer, left means a negative answer: 2 − 5 is the jump from 5 to 2, 3 steps LEFT, so −3. Second example if time: −2 − (−8) is the jump from −8 to −2: 6 right, so 6. Do NOT teach "two minuses make a plus" as a rule today; let them see it.

p6l3-try2.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Whiteboards. a) Move 7 left from 3: −4. b) From −2 to 6: 2 + 6 = 8 steps right, so 8. c) From −9 to −5: 4 steps right, so 4. Check each by adding back: −2 + 8 = 6, −9 + 4 = −5.

p6l3-key.note: Minutes 35.5 to 36.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Ordering negatives by their digits (saying −9 > −4). (2) Crossing zero wrongly: 3 − 8 answered as 5 or −11 (split the jump at 0). (3) In code, using "change by 1" when the variable should go down, or counting the start value as one of the repeats when tracing.

p6l3-break.note: Minutes 36.5 to 41.5. 5 minutes. Floors after each move: 3, −2, −4, 2. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p6l3-ws1.note: Minutes 41.5 to 54.5. Paper only for page 1 (laptops closed or turned away). Walk around (online: visit breakout rooms). Ask "Which way did you move? Where did you cross zero?" before giving help. Show this preview, do not read it aloud.

p6l3-ws1ans.note: Minutes 54.5 to 57.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q1 (which is bigger, −4 or −9, and why), about 35 seconds a question. Q1c: −4 > −9 because −4 is further right (warmer). Q2b: −24 up to −13 is 11. Q2e: 13 up to 0, then 31 more: 44. Q3a: from −6 up to 9 is 6 + 9 = 15 m. Q3c: −6 + 4 = −2, then −2 − 11 = −13 m.

p6l3-teachtrace.note: Minutes 57.5 to 60.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 traces a program, and the second panel is the Q6 bug hunt). Click to fill each row while the children call out the value: 20 − 15 = 5, 5 − 15 = −10, −10 − 15 = −25. Point out: the "start" row is not one of the repeats. The "say" block is outside the loop, so it only speaks once, at the end. Optional Python version of this trace: x = 20 | for i in range(3): x = x - 15 | print(x) (prints -25). Bug hunt for Q6 and the Q7 plan (second panel): Ravi wants a countdown that says 3, 2, 1, 0, −1 but his code says 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Ask first: "Which block is wrong? How do you know?" Only one block needs to change: change n by −1. Show that 5 repeats are still right (3, 2, 1, 0, −1 is five numbers). Planning tip for Q7: write the start value, how many repeats and the change each time.

p6l3-ws2.note: Minutes 60.5 to 70.5. Children work alone. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Paper first, then they may build Q5 to Q7 in Scratch to test their answers. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p6l3-ws2ans.note: Minutes 70.5 to 74.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q5 (the trace). Q4e: from −3 to 5 is 8 steps right. Q4f: from −7 to −1 is 6 steps right. Q5b: −80 to −200 is 120 more, and 120 ÷ 30 = 4. Q6a: 5 + 8 = 13 (the lift goes UP to floor 13). Q6c: 5 − 8 = −3, the third basement. Q7: 7 × 4 = 28, so 7 repeats reach −28; to come back up in one block, change depth by 28.

p6l3-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Answers: 1) It rose 11 degrees (4 up to 0, then 7). At 10 p.m.: 7 − 9 = −2 °C. 2) −10 (10 − 4 × 5 = 10 − 20 = −10). 3) −3: the gap is 12, half is 6, and −9 + 6 = −3 (check: 3 − 6 = −3).

p6l3-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) One answer: top row −3, 2, 1; middle row 4, 0, −4; bottom row −1, −2, 3 (0 must be in the middle; there are 8 answers, all turns and flips of this one). 2) 17 °C: midnight to 7 a.m. is 7 hours, −6 + 14 = 8 °C; 7 a.m. to 10 a.m. is 3 hours, 8 + 9 = 17 °C.

p6l3-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Which pairs of tiles add to 0? Where must 0 go? For Q2: count the hops of each colour before adding anything.

p6l3-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: check every line of the finished square aloud: rows −3 + 2 + 1, 4 + 0 − 4, −1 − 2 + 3; columns −3 + 4 − 1, 2 + 0 − 2, 1 − 4 + 3; diagonals −3 + 0 + 3, 1 + 0 − 1. All 0. Why 4 is not in a corner: the two numbers with it must make −4, and only −4 with 0 or −3 with −1 do that, but a corner is in three lines. Q2: a common mistake is 10 hops of +2 (−6 + 20 = 14). Code idea: set t to −6, repeat 7 change t by 2, repeat 3 change t by 3, say t.

p6l3-talk.note: Minutes 77.5 to 83.5. Both questions are kept in this lesson (it has the flex). Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: No. −8 is further left on the number line, so it is smaller: −8 °C is colder than −3 °C, and floor −8 is lower than floor −3. The digits 8 and 3 tell us how FAR from 0, not which side. Praise reasons that use a picture or a real example. Second question if time: "Why does change by −3 make a number go down?"

p6l3-exit.note: Minutes 83.5 to 86. Answer: −5 °C (−3 − 6 = −9, then −9 + 4 = −5). Extension: write a Scratch program that starts temp at −3 and shows each change, then try it.

p6l3-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
